svg.title: How 802.1Q double tagging crosses a VLAN boundary, why the flight is one-way, and the three settings that close it
svg.desc: Top: a frame drawn field by field as the attacker sends it - destination MAC, source MAC, outer tag of VLAN 999 which is the native VLAN, inner tag of VLAN 20 which is the target, then the payload. Switch one receives it on an access port in VLAN 999, sees its native VLAN and strips the outer tag without inspecting the inner one, then forwards the frame onto the trunk. Switch two sees a frame tagged VLAN 20 and delivers it. The consequence is a one-way jump: the attacker can send into VLAN 20 but replies are routed back to VLAN 999 where the attacker's address does not exist, so this is a stepping stone for one-way injection, not a working MITM. Middle: the two other routes - DTP negotiation, where an access port is talked into becoming a trunk, and a trunk left enabled by mistake during installation. Bottom: three settings and the reasoning - switchport mode access plus nonegotiate on every access port, a dedicated unused native VLAN with no SVI and no access port, and forcing tagging on trunks with dot1q tag native where supported.
svg.text: VLAN hopping by double tagging: the outer tag is the one the first switch strips
The attack only works because the native VLAN arrives untagged in the switch's own logic - so the native VLAN is the whole vulnerability
THE FRAME AS THE ATTACKER SENDS IT

g.text: the switch never looks this far
sees native VLAN, strips outer tag

svg.text: Why it is a one-way jump:
the reply from VLAN 20 is routed or switched back inside VLAN 20, where the attacker has no address. Useful for injecting one-way traffic
(spoofed management commands, one-shot exploit, DHCP or DNS poisoning), not for a working man in the middle. Design reviews often overstate it - the fix is still mandatory.
THE OTHER TWO ROUTES INTO ANOTHER VLAN
DTP negotiation
The attacker sends DTP frames and the access port is talked into becoming a trunk,
which hands over every allowed VLAN at once. Fix: switchport mode access plus
switchport nonegotiate on every port that is not deliberately a trunk.
A trunk left enabled by mistake
An installation template that pushes switchport mode trunk. Fix: port templates
THE THREE SETTINGS THAT CLOSE IT
1 · Dedicated native VLAN
switchport trunk native vlan 999 where 999 has no SVI
and appears on no access port - so a successful hop
lands in an empty VLAN with nothing to attack
2 · Nonegotiate everywhere
3 · vlan dot1q tag native where supported
forces the native VLAN to be tagged, killing the premise

The design test: open the trunk configuration of any production switch and look for a native VLAN that also has an SVI. If it does, the native VLAN is carrying service and the whole mitigation is cosmetic.
Second test: does any port template still allow DTP to negotiate? That is a one-command fix with a five-year payoff.
